title: Twenty-one years at one gig, family security and job offers
summary: A steady job let him raise two children; he turned down Woody Herman, Stan Kenton and Jimmy Dorsey, and visitors considered the DeLisa and Chez Paree musts.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Well, the 21 years, one gig, is an awfully long time.
Your little bio here, you say that's a record. I guess it is.
Yeah, right. But, well, see, it's a long time, but it's according to what your ambitions are. I started out, I had two sons, two children, and it pretty much --
-- steady gig allowed you to spend time with your family.

Family, right. And then it gives you a little more security that you would have to do, I mean, would have. Because I was offered a lot of jobs, like with Woody. I could have stayed with Woody, Stan Kenton, he asked me -- oh, man, he almost got on his knees. This was during the band days, and everything was going -- and Jimmy Dorsey, I could have been with Jimmy Dorsey's band.
So all of these was the thing, but --
They would come out to the club.
Well, it was a national reputation from people who visited. I mean, during that time, your trip into Chicago was not complete unless you went to the Chez

Paris and the Delisa. Because that's just the way it was. These were the two things. And every musician would come out there, because they had kicks. It was a good joint, good time. No pressure on you or nothing like that, and could do what they wanted to and whatever.
So it was really a -- we don't have those type of places anymore.
Well, it was a different time.
